questions.question: Volume percentage (v/v) of a liquid solute dissolved in a liquid solvent is defined as:
options: C) \( \frac{\text{Volume of solute}}{\text{Total mass of solution}} \times 100 \)
D) \( \frac{\text{Volume of solute}}{\text{Total volume of solution}} \times 100 \)
questions.explanation: Volume percentage is volume of solute divided by total volume of solution multiplied by 100.

questions.question: A binary mixture of liquids that boils at a constant temperature and distills without any change in composition is called an:
questions.explanation: Azeotropes are binary liquid mixtures having the same composition in both liquid and vapour phases, boiling at a single constant temperature.

questions.sub_topic: Ideal Solution Thermodynamic Criterion: Delta S and Delta G
questions.question: For the formation of an ideal binary solution at constant temperature and pressure, the thermodynamic entropy and Gibbs free energy of mixing are:
questions.explanation: Spontaneous mixing always increases disorder (\( \Delta_{\text{mix}} S > 0 \)). Since \( \Delta_{\text{mix}} H = 0 \) for ideal solutions, \( \Delta_{\text{mix}} G = \Delta H - T\Delta S = -T\Delta S < 0 \).

questions.sub_topic: Molar Mass from Freezing Point Depression Calculation
questions.question: When 1.80 g of a non-volatile non-electrolyte solute is dissolved in 90.0 g of benzene, the freezing point is depressed by 0.50 K. The molar mass of the solute is: (\( K_f \) of benzene = 5.00 K kg/mol)
questions.explanation: \( M_2 = \frac{K_f \cdot w_2 \cdot 1000}{\Delta T_f \cdot w_1} = \frac{5.00 \times 1.80 \times 1000}{0.50 \times 90.0} = \frac{9000}{45} = 200 \text{ g/mol} \).

questions.sub_topic: Abnormal Colligative Property of Potassium Sulfate
questions.question: What is the expected boiling point of a 0.1 m aqueous solution of potassium sulfate (\( \ce{K2SO4} \)) assuming 90% dissociation? (\( K_b \) of water = 0.52 K kg/mol)
In standard IUPAC notation for representing a galvanic cell, the phase boundary between electrode and electrolyte solution is shown by a:
questions.explanation: A single vertical line represents a phase boundary (e.g. \( \ce{Zn(s) | Zn^{2+}(aq)} \)), while a double vertical line represents the salt bridge.

questions.question: The difference between the actual potential required for electrolytic gas discharge and the reversible thermodynamic potential is termed:
questions.explanation: Overpotential is the extra potential beyond the thermodynamic equilibrium value required to overcome kinetic activation barriers at the electrode.

questions.question: The SI unit of molar conductivity (\( \Lambda_m \)) is:
questions.explanation: \( \Lambda_m = \kappa / c = \frac{\text{S m}^{-1}}{\text{mol m}^{-3}} = \text{S m}^2 \text{mol}^{-1} \).

questions.question: In the alkaline \( \ce{H2-O2} \) fuel cell, the oxidation reaction taking place at the anode is:
questions.explanation: In alkaline fuel cell (conc. aqueous KOH electrolyte), hydrogen gas is oxidized at the anode: \( \ce{2H2 + 4OH^- -> 4H2O + 4e^-} \).

questions.question: The cell \( \ce{Ag(s) | Ag+(sat. AgBr) || Ag+(0.1 M) | Ag(s)} \) exhibits a potential of 0.414 V at 298 K. The solubility product (\( K_{sp} \)) of \( \ce{AgBr} \) is:
questions.explanation: \( E_{\text{cell}} = 0.0591 \log \frac{0.1}{[\ce{Ag+}]_1} \Rightarrow 0.414 = 0.0591 \log \frac{0.1}{[\ce{Ag+}]_1} \Rightarrow \log \frac{0.1}{[\ce{Ag+}]_1} = 7 \Rightarrow [\ce{Ag+}]_1 = 10^{-8} \text{ M} \). For \( \ce{AgBr} \), \( K_{sp} = [\ce{Ag+}][\ce{Br-}] = (10^{-8})^2 = 1.0 \times 10^{-16} \).

questions.question: For a zero-order chemical reaction \( \ce{A -> B} \), doubling the initial concentration of reactant A causes the reaction rate to:
questions.explanation: Since \( \text{Rate} = k [A]^0 = k \), the rate is independent of reactant concentration and remains unchanged.

questions.sub_topic: Endothermic Reaction Activation Energy Energy Profile
questions.question: For an endothermic chemical reaction (\( \Delta H > 0 \)), the activation energy of the forward reaction (\( E_{a,f} \)) is:
options: A) Always less than the activation energy of the backward reaction
B) Exactly equal to the activation energy of the backward reaction
D) Always greater than the activation energy of the backward reaction (\( E_{a,b} \))
questions.explanation: Since \( \Delta H = E_{a,f} - E_{a,b} \), for an endothermic reaction (\( \Delta H > 0 \)), \( E_{a,f} = E_{a,b} + \Delta H > E_{a,b} \).

questions.sub_topic: Determination of Order from Half-Life Data
questions.question: When the initial concentration of a reactant is tripled, its half-life period decreases to one-third. The order of the reaction is:
questions.explanation: \( t_{1/2} \propto 1/[A]_0^{n-1} \). Here, tripling \( [A]_0 \) reduces \( t_{1/2} \) by factor of 3 (\( 1/3 \)), meaning \( t_{1/2} \propto 1/[A]_0 \). Thus \( n - 1 = 1 \Rightarrow n = 2 \).

questions.sub_topic: Rate Law from Reaction Mechanism with Fast Equilibrium
questions.question: For the reaction \( \ce{2NO + O2 -> 2NO2} \), the proposed mechanism is: \( \ce{2NO <=> N2O2} \) (fast, \( K_{\text{eq}} \)) and \( \ce{N2O2 + O2 ->[k_2] 2NO2} \) (slow). The rate law is:
questions.explanation: \( \text{Rate} = k_2 [\ce{N2O2}][\ce{O2}] \). From fast pre-equilibrium, \( [\ce{N2O2}] = K_{\text{eq}}[\ce{NO}]^2 \). Substituting gives \( \text{Rate} = k_2 K_{\text{eq}}[\ce{NO}]^2[\ce{O2}] = k[\ce{NO}]^2[\ce{O2}] \).

questions.sub_topic: Arrhenius Temperature Ratio Calculation for 10-Fold Acceleration
questions.question: A reaction has activation energy \( E_a = 95.7 \text{ kJ/mol} \). By how much must the temperature increase from 300 K to increase the rate by a factor of 10? (\( R = 8.314 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{mol}^{-1} \))
questions.explanation: \( \log 10 = 1 = \frac{E_a}{2.303 R} \left( \frac{T_2 - 300}{300 T_2} \right) \Rightarrow 1 = \frac{95700}{19.147} \left( \frac{T_2 - 300}{300 T_2} \right) = 5000 \left( \frac{T_2 - 300}{300 T_2} \right) \Rightarrow 300 T_2 = 5000 T_2 - 1.5 \times 10^6 \Rightarrow 4700 T_2 = 1.5 \times 10^6 \Rightarrow T_2 \approx 319.1 \text{ K} \approx 320 \text{ K} \) (increase of ~20 K).

questions.topic: Unit IV: d and f Block Elements
questions.question: Across the 3d transition series from scandium to copper, the density of metals generally:
options: A) Decreases steadily across the period
B) Increases steadily, reaching a maximum near copper
C) Remains constant for all elements
D) Reaches a sharp minimum at chromium
questions.explanation: Atomic mass increases while metallic atomic volume decreases due to increasing nuclear charge, resulting in a steady increase in density from Sc (3.1 g/cm³) to Cu (8.9 g/cm³).

questions.topic: Unit IV: d and f Block Elements
questions.sub_topic: Oxidation State of Manganese in Permanganate
questions.question: What is the oxidation state of manganese in potassium permanganate (\( \ce{KMnO4} \))?
questions.explanation: In \( \ce{KMnO4} \): \( +1 + x + 4(-2) = 0 \Rightarrow x - 7 = 0 \Rightarrow x = +7 \).

questions.topic: Unit IV: d and f Block Elements
questions.sub_topic: Preparation of Potassium Dichromate from Chromite Ore
questions.question: In the industrial manufacture of potassium dichromate, chromite ore (\( \ce{FeCr2O4} \)) is first roasted with sodium carbonate in excess air to yield:
questions.explanation: \( \ce{4FeCr2O4 + 8Na2CO3 + 7O2 -> 8Na2CrO4 + 2Fe2O3 + 8CO2} \). The resulting yellow solution of \( \ce{Na2CrO4} \) is then acidified to produce \( \ce{Na2Cr2O7} \).

questions.topic: Unit IV: d and f Block Elements
questions.sub_topic: Interstitial Compounds Hardness and Melting Point
questions.question: Interstitial hydrides and carbides of transition metals (such as \( \ce{TiC} \) and \( \ce{WC} \)) possess melting points that are:
options: A) Higher than those of the pure parent transition metals
D) Zero on the Celsius scale
questions.explanation: Trapping small non-metal atoms (H, B, C, N) inside octahedral lattice holes impedes metallic plane slipping and introduces directional bonding, increasing hardness and melting point.

questions.topic: Unit IV: d and f Block Elements
questions.sub_topic: Oxidizing Power of Oxo-Cations in Actinoids
questions.question: Uranium, neptunium, and plutonium form stable dioxo actinyl cations of the type \( \ce{MO2^{2+}} \). The geometry and bonding in these uranyl-type ions involve:
options: A) Bent geometry with 104.5° bond angle
B) Purely ionic electrostatic attraction between isolated ions
C) Tetrahedral coordination around an empty nucleus
D) Linear O=M=O geometry with strong covalent pi-bonding involving 5f and 6d orbitals
questions.explanation: The \( \ce{UO2^{2+}} \) cation is linear [O-U-O]²⁺ with short, strong axial U-O bonds involving overlap of uranium 5f and 6d orbitals with oxygen 2p orbitals.

questions.question: A di- or polydentate ligand that uses two or more donor atoms to bind a single metal ion to form a ring structure is called a:
questions.explanation: When a multidentate ligand coordinates simultaneously to a single central metal ion, forming a 5- or 6-membered chelate ring, it is termed a chelating ligand.

questions.question: Tetracarbonylnickel(0), \( [\ce{Ni(CO)4}] \), is diamagnetic and has which geometry and hybridization?
questions.explanation: Ni(0) has configuration \( 3d^8 4s^2 \). Strong ligand \( \ce{CO} \) forces the two 4s electrons into the 3d orbitals to give a completely filled \( 3d^{10} \) subshell, leaving 4s and 4p for \( sp^3 \) tetrahedral hybridization.

questions.sub_topic: Hydrate Isomers of Chromium Chloride Hexahydrate
questions.question: When excess silver nitrate is added to an aqueous solution containing 1 mole of \( [\ce{Cr(H2O)5Cl}]\ce{Cl2.H2O} \), the number of moles of \( \ce{AgCl} \) precipitated is:
questions.explanation: Only the chloride ions present in the outer ionization sphere as counter ions ionize in water; with 2 counter chlorides, exactly 2 moles of \( \ce{AgCl} \) precipitate.

questions.sub_topic: Crystal Field Splitting: Octahedral vs Tetrahedral Magnitude
questions.question: If the crystal field splitting energy (\( \Delta_o \)) for an octahedral complex is 18,000 cm⁻¹, the expected splitting energy (\( \Delta_t \)) for the corresponding tetrahedral complex is:
questions.explanation: \( \Delta_t = \frac{4}{9} \Delta_o = \frac{4}{9} \times 18000 = 8000 \text{ cm}^{-1} \).

questions.sub_topic: Spin-Only Moment of Low-Spin Octahedral Cobalt(III)
questions.question: The complex ion \( [\ce{Co(NH3)6}]^{3+} \) is diamagnetic (\( \mu = 0 \)) because:
options: A) \( \ce{Co^{3+}} \) is \( 3d^6 \), and strong-field \( \ce{NH3} \) ligands force all 6 electrons to pair up in the lower \( t_{2g} \) orbitals
B) Cobalt in this complex has lost all its d-electrons
C) The complex is square planar with \( dsp^2 \) hybridization
D) Ammonia donates protons that cancel electronic spins
questions.explanation: In \( [\ce{Co(NH3)6}]^{3+} \), \( \Delta_o > P \); all six 3d electrons pair up in \( t_{2g} \) (\( t_{2g}^6 e_g^0 \)), leaving zero unpaired electrons and conferring diamagnetism.

questions.sub_topic: Dipole Moment of Alkyl Halides Polar Nature
questions.question: The carbon-halogen bond in haloalkanes is polar because:
options: A) Carbon atoms form coordinate covalent bonds with hydrogen
B) Halogens lose electrons spontaneously to carbon
C) Halogen atoms are significantly more electronegative than carbon, acquiring a partial negative charge
D) Alkyl halides exist exclusively as ionic gases
questions.explanation: Halogens have higher electronegativity than carbon, pulling shared electron density towards themselves (\( \ce{C^{\delta+} - X^{\delta-}} \)), creating a permanent molecular dipole.

questions.question: Dry acetone is specifically chosen as the solvent in the Finkelstein reaction because:
options: A) Acetone dissolves NaCl and NaBr to form clear solutions
B) Sodium iodide (NaI) is soluble in dry acetone, whereas NaCl and NaBr precipitate out, driving the reaction forward
C) Acetone decomposes alkyl halides into alkenes
D) NaI is completely insoluble in dry acetone
questions.explanation: According to Le Chatelier's principle, precipitation of \( \ce{NaCl} \) or \( \ce{NaBr} \) in dry acetone shifts the equilibrium forward to yield the alkyl iodide.

questions.question: The reactivity of primary, secondary, and tertiary alcohols with concentrated \( \ce{HCl} \) and anhydrous \( \ce{ZnCl2} \) (Lucas test) follows the order:
questions.explanation: The reaction proceeds via carbocation intermediates (\( \text{S}_\text{N}1 \)). Carbocation stability order (3° > 2° > 1°) dictates the rate of turbidity formation.

questions.question: Heating chloroethane with silver fluoride (\( \ce{AgF} \)) yields fluoroethane and silver chloride precipitate. This halogen-exchange reaction is termed the:
questions.explanation: The Swarts reaction is the standard method for preparing alkyl fluorides by heating alkyl chlorides or bromides with heavy metal fluorides (\( \ce{AgF, Hg2F2, CoF3, SbF3} \)).

questions.question: Dehydrohalogenation of 2-bromobutane with alcoholic \( \ce{KOH} \) yields a mixture of but-2-ene (81%) and but-1-ene (19%). This regiochemical preference is governed by:
options: A) Hofmann's rule (formation of the least substituted alkene)
B) Saytzeff's rule (formation of the more substituted, thermodynamically more stable alkene)
C) Markovnikov's rule of electrophilic addition
questions.explanation: Saytzeff's rule governs \( \beta \)-elimination with unhindered bases: the hydrogen is eliminated from the \( \beta \)-carbon having fewer hydrogens, yielding the more stable internal alkene (but-2-ene).

questions.topic: Unit VII: Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
questions.sub_topic: Distinction of Alcohols using Lucas Reagent
questions.question: A secondary alcohol treated with Lucas reagent at room temperature produces turbidity after approximately:
questions.explanation: Secondary alcohols react at a moderate rate via carbocations, producing turbidity (insoluble alkyl chloride) within ~5 minutes at room temperature.

questions.topic: Unit VII: Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
questions.question: Williamson ether synthesis involves the reaction between:
options: B) An alkyl halide and a sodium alkoxide
C) An aldehyde and an alcohol
D) A ketone and a Grignard reagent
questions.explanation: Williamson synthesis is an \( \text{S}_\text{N}2 \) displacement of a primary alkyl halide by an alkoxide ion: \( \ce{R-X + R'-ONa -> R-O-R' + NaX} \).

questions.topic: Unit VII: Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
questions.question: Why is 4-nitrophenol a stronger acid than 4-methoxyphenol?
options: B) The methoxy group forms covalent bonds with water
D) The nitro group (-NO2) is electron-withdrawing (-M, -I) stabilizing the phenoxide, while the methoxy group (-OCH3) is electron-releasing (+M) destabilizing it
questions.explanation: The strong -M and -I effects of the nitro group delocalize and stabilize the negative charge in phenoxide. The methoxy group donates electron density (+M), destabilizing phenoxide and reducing acidity.

questions.topic: Unit VII: Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
questions.question: When sodium phenoxide is heated with carbon dioxide under pressure followed by acidification, the major product is:
questions.explanation: In Kolbe's reaction, electrophilic attack of \( \ce{CO2} \) on sodium phenoxide at 400 K and 4-7 atm yields sodium salicylate, which upon acidification gives salicylic acid.

questions.topic: Unit VII: Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
questions.sub_topic: Cleavage of Phenyl Alkyl Ethers with HI Mechanism
questions.question: When methoxybenzene (anisole) is heated with concentrated hydroiodic acid (HI), phenol and iodobenzene are NOT formed; instead, phenol and methyl iodide are formed because:
options: A) The C_aryl-O bond has partial double-bond character due to resonance and cannot be cleaved, forcing iodide to attack the methyl group
B) Methyl iodide is a gas that escapes
C) Phenol is insoluble in acid
D) Iodine atoms cannot bond to aromatic rings
questions.explanation: In anisole, resonance between oxygen lone pairs and the aromatic ring imparts partial double-bond character to the \( \ce{C_{aryl}-O} \) bond, resisting cleavage; nucleophilic attack occurs on the \( sp^3 \) methyl carbon.

questions.topic: Unit VIII: Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids
questions.sub_topic: Reduction of Carbonyl Group: Clemmensen Reaction
questions.question: In the Clemmensen reduction, a carbonyl compound is converted to a methylene group (\( \ce{>C=O -> >CH2} \)) using:
options: A) Hydrazine and potassium hydroxide in ethylene glycol
B) Lithium aluminium hydride in ether
questions.explanation: Clemmensen reduction uses zinc amalgam (\( \ce{Zn-Hg} \)) in concentrated hydrochloric acid to reduce aldehydes and ketones to alkanes.

questions.topic: Unit VIII: Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids
questions.question: Aldehydes that lack an \( \alpha \)-hydrogen atom undergo self-oxidation and self-reduction in concentrated alkali to yield an alcohol and a carboxylate salt. This reaction is known as the:
questions.explanation: The Cannizzaro reaction is the disproportionation of non-enolizable aldehydes (such as formaldehyde and benzaldehyde) in strong base to form a primary alcohol and a carboxylic acid salt.

questions.topic: Unit VIII: Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids
questions.question: Arrange acetic acid, monochloroacetic acid, dichloroacetic acid, and trichloroacetic acid in order of decreasing acidic strength:
options: A) Acetic acid > Monochloroacetic acid > Dichloroacetic acid > Trichloroacetic acid
B) Monochloroacetic acid > Dichloroacetic acid > Trichloroacetic acid > Acetic acid
C) Trichloroacetic acid > Dichloroacetic acid > Monochloroacetic acid > Acetic acid
D) Dichloroacetic acid > Trichloroacetic acid > Monochloroacetic acid > Acetic acid
questions.explanation: Greater number of electron-withdrawing chlorine atoms exerts stronger inductive (-I) effect, stabilizing the carboxylate anion and increasing acidity: \( \ce{CCl3COOH > CHCl2COOH > CH2ClCOOH > CH3COOH} \).

questions.topic: Unit VIII: Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids
questions.question: In the Etard reaction, toluene is oxidized to benzaldehyde using chromyl chloride (\( \ce{CrO2Cl2} \)) in carbon disulfide solvent through the formation of:
options: A) A brown chromium coordination complex which is subsequently hydrolyzed with water
B) A benzoic acid precipitate directly
questions.explanation: \( \ce{CrO2Cl2} \) oxidizes the methyl group to a brown insoluble chromium complex \( \ce{C6H5CH(OCrOHCl2)2} \), which on hydrolysis yields benzaldehyde.

questions.topic: Unit VIII: Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids
questions.sub_topic: Crossed Aldol Condensation: Benzaldehyde and Acetophenone
questions.question: Reaction of benzaldehyde with acetophenone in the presence of dilute sodium hydroxide at room temperature yields:
questions.explanation: Acetophenone has \( \alpha \)-hydrogens and forms an enolate that attacks the non-enolizable benzaldehyde carbonyl; dehydration of the resulting \( \beta \)-hydroxyketone yields the conjugated enone chalcone (Claisen-Schmidt reaction).

questions.question: Trimethylamine (\( (\ce{CH3})_3\ce{N} \)) is classified as a:
questions.explanation: All three hydrogen atoms of ammonia are replaced by methyl groups, making trimethylamine a tertiary amine.

questions.sub_topic: Hoffmann Bromamide Degradation Substrate and Product
questions.question: In the Hoffmann bromamide degradation reaction, treating an acid amide with bromine and alkali produces:
options: A) A secondary amine containing the same number of carbon atoms
B) A tertiary amine with one carbon atom more
D) A primary amine containing one carbon atom less than the parent amide
questions.explanation: Hoffmann degradation: \( \ce{R-CONH2 + Br2 + 4NaOH -> R-NH2 + Na2CO3 + 2NaBr + 2H2O} \). The product amine has one carbon atom less than the amide.

questions.sub_topic: Basicity: Methylamines in Gaseous vs Aqueous Medium
questions.question: Why does the basic strength order of methyl-substituted amines in aqueous solution (\( 2^\circ > 1^\circ > 3^\circ > \ce{NH3} \)) differ from that in the gaseous phase (\( 3^\circ > 2^\circ > 1^\circ > \ce{NH3} \))?
options: A) Water decomposes tertiary amines into ammonia gas
B) In aqueous solution, hydration energy of the conjugate ammonium cations and steric hindrance combine with the inductive effect
C) Methyl groups reverse their dipole moments in liquid water
D) Secondary amines are completely non-polar in gas phase
questions.explanation: In gas phase, only inductive effect (+I) operates. In water, hydration stability of the conjugate cation (1° > 2° > 3°) opposes the inductive trend, producing the intermediate 2° > 1° > 3° order for methylamines.

questions.question: Which of the following amines will produce a positive result (foul-smelling isocyanide) in the carbylamine test?
questions.explanation: Only primary amines (both aliphatic and aromatic) give the carbylamine test with \( \ce{CHCl3} \) and alcoholic \( \ce{KOH} \). Aniline is a primary aromatic amine.

questions.question: When benzenediazonium chloride is coupled with 2-naphthol (\( \beta \)-naphthol) in alkaline medium, the azo dye is formed by substitution at position:
questions.explanation: The 1-position of 2-naphthol is strongly activated by the adjacent 2-hydroxyl group and experiences maximum electron density and favorable wheland intermediate stability.

questions.question: Glucose and fructose are structural isomers having the same molecular formula (\( \ce{C6H12O6} \)), but glucose is an aldohexose while fructose is a:
questions.explanation: Glucose contains an aldehyde functional group (aldohexose), whereas fructose contains a ketone functional group at C-2 (ketohexose).

questions.question: In neutral aqueous solution, an \( \alpha \)-amino acid exists as a dipolar zwitterion having the structural formula:
questions.explanation: Internal acid-base neutralization transfers a proton from the carboxyl group to the amino group, forming the dipolar zwitterion \( \ce{^+H3N-CHR-COO^-} \).

questions.sub_topic: Hydrogen Bonding in Secondary Structure of Proteins
questions.question: In the \( \alpha \)-helix secondary structure of proteins, hydrogen bonds form between the carbonyl oxygen of each amino acid residue and the amide hydrogen of the:
options: B) Tenth amino acid residue down the chain
C) Fourth amino acid residue down the chain (n + 4 residue)
questions.explanation: In an \( \alpha \)-helix, each turn has 3.6 amino acid residues; the \( \ce{C=O} \) of residue \( n \) forms a hydrogen bond with the \( \ce{N-H} \) of residue \( n+4 \).

questions.sub_topic: Differences between DNA and RNA Sugars
questions.question: The pentose sugar present in DNA is 2-deoxy-D-ribose, which differs from D-ribose (in RNA) by lacking an oxygen atom at carbon:
questions.explanation: 2-Deoxy-D-ribose lacks the hydroxyl oxygen at carbon 2' (having two hydrogens at C-2'), whereas D-ribose has an -OH group at C-2'.

questions.question: Vitamin B2 (riboflavin) is biologically active as the prosthetic coenzyme group in which redox carriers?
options: A) FMN (Flavin Mononucleotide) and FAD (Flavin Adenine Dinucleotide)
questions.explanation: Riboflavin is the dietary precursor for the flavin cofactors FMN and FAD, which participate as prosthetic electron carriers in cellular respiration.
